title.en: The Sixteen Lands of Ahura Mazda
title.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達的十六國土

region.zh: 雅利安維耶迦（象徵位置：高加索阿蘭）

texts.period: Vendidad, Fargard I; Avestan, c. 1000-600 BCE (trans. Darmesteter, 1895)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 4: The Zend-Avesta, Part I, The Vendidad, Fargard I (trans. James Darmesteter)

summary.en: Ahura Mazda enumerates to Zarathustra the sixteen good lands he created, each marred in its turn by the counter-creations of Angra Mainyu, 'who is all death': the first, Airyanem Vaego by the Vanguhi Daitya, receives the serpent in the river and ten months of winter; and in four-cornered Varena was Thraetaona born, who smote the dragon Azi Dahaka.
summary.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達向瑣羅亞斯德細數所造十六善土，而「即死亡」的安格拉·曼紐逐一以反造毀之：首土雅利安維耶迦臨達伊提亞河，得河中之蛇與十月寒冬；四角之瓦雷納生了誅龍者特勞塔奧納。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text:
Ahura Mazda spake unto Spitama Zarathustra, saying: I have made every land dear (to its people), even though it had no charms whatever in it: had I not made every land dear (to its people), even though it had no charms whatever in it, then the whole living world would have invaded the Airyana Vaego.
The first of the good lands and countries which I, Ahura Mazda, created, was the Airyana Vaego, by the Vanguhi Daitya. Thereupon came Angra Mainyu, who is all death, and he counter-created the serpent in the river and Winter, a work of the Daêvas.
There are ten winter months there, two summer months; and those are cold for the waters, cold for the earth, cold for the trees. Winter falls there, the worst of all plagues.

The fourteenth of the good lands and countries which I, Ahura Mazda, created, was the four-cornered Varena, for which was born Thraetaona, who smote Azi Dahaka. Thereupon came Angra Mainyu, who is all death, and he counter-created abnormal issues in women and barbarian oppression.

title.en: Yima and the Vara Against the Deadly Winter
title.zh: 伊瑪與避冬之瓦拉

region.zh: 雅利安維耶迦（象徵位置：撒馬爾罕）

texts.period: Vendidad, Fargard II; Avestan, c. 1000-600 BCE (trans. Darmesteter, 1895)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 4: The Vendidad, Fargard II (trans. James Darmesteter)

summary.en: The fair Yima, the good shepherd, refuses to preach the Religion but agrees to nourish the world, where for his sway there is 'neither cold wind nor hot wind, neither disease nor death'; warned of deadly winters to come, he builds the Vara and brings into it, two of every kind, the seeds of men, cattle, trees, and fires, to live the happiest life until the earth is renewed.
summary.zh: 美裔牧者伊瑪拒傳其教，卻允養育世界——其治下「無寒風無熱風，無病無死」；得預警毀滅性寒冬將至，遂築地下瓦拉，攜人畜樹火之種各二入內，安居極樂，以候大地更新。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Ahura Mazda answered: The fair Yima, the good shepherd, O holy Zarathustra! he was the first mortal, before thee, Zarathustra, with whom I, Ahura Mazda, did converse, whom I taught the Religion of Ahura, the Religion of Zarathustra. Unto him, O Zarathustra, I, Ahura Mazda, spake, saying: 'Well, fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, be thou the preacher and the bearer of my Religion!' And the fair Yima, O Zarathusra, replied unto me, saying: 'I was not born, I was not taught to be the preacher and the bearer of thy Religion.'

O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat! Upon the material world the evil winters are about to fall, that shall bring the fierce, deadly frost; upon the material world the evil winters are about to fall, that shall make snow-flakes fall thick, even an aredvi deep on the highest tops of mountains. Therefore make thee a Vara, long as a riding-ground on every side of the square, and thither bring the seeds of sheep and oxen, of men, of dogs, of birds, and of red blazing fires.

Thither thou shalt bring the seeds of men and women, of the greatest, best, and finest on this earth; thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of cattle, of the greatest, best, and finest on this earth. Thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of tree, of the highest of size and sweetest of odour on this earth; thither thou shalt bring the seeds of every kind of fruit, the best of savour and sweetest of odour. All those seeds shalt thou bring, two of every kind, to be kept inexhaustible there, so long as those men shall stay in the Vara.

title.en: The Bundahishn: The Covenant of the Two Spirits
title.zh: 邦達希申：二靈之約

region.zh: 法爾斯（波斯帕薩，伊朗）

texts.period: Bundahishn, Pahlavi, c. 7th-9th c. CE (trans. West, 1880)

source.work: Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 5: Pahlavi Texts, Part I, The Bundahis, ch. 1 (trans. E. W. West)

summary.en: The Zoroastrian cosmology opens with the two spirits: Auharmazd in endless light, omniscient and good; Aharman in the endlessly dark abyss, 'with backward understanding and desire for destruction.' Foreseeing the end, Auharmazd recites the Ahunavar that confounds the evil spirit, and creates within his confusion the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, and mankind.
summary.zh: 祆教宇宙論開篇即二靈：奧哈爾馬茲達居無盡光明，全知至善；阿哈爾曼居無盡黑暗之淵，「悟性倒錯，志在毀滅」。奧哈爾馬茲達預知終局，誦阿胡納瓦爾咒使惡靈昏亂，並於其昏亂中造天、水、地、植、獸與人。

sensitivity.note: Living scriptural tradition of Zoroastrianism. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: As revealed by the religion of the Mazdayasnians, so it is declared that Auharmazd is supreme in omniscience and goodness, and unrivalled in splendour; the region of light is the place of Auharmazd, which they call 'endless light,' and the omniscience and goodness of the unrivalled Auharmazd is what they call 'revelation.' Revelation is the explanation of both spirits together; one is he who is independent of unlimited time, because Auharmazd and the region, religion, and time of Auharmazd were and are and ever will be; while Aharman in darkness, with backward understanding and desire for destruction, was in the abyss, and 'it is he who will not be; and the place of that destruction, and also of that darkness, is what they call the 'endlessly dark.' And between them was empty space, that is, what they call 'air,' in which is now their meeting.

Auharmazd also knew this, through omniscience, that within these nine thousand years, for three thousand years everything proceeds by the will of Auharmazd, three thousand years there is an intermingling of the wills of Auharmazd and Aharman, and the last three thousand years the evil spirit is disabled, and they keep the adversary away from the creatures. Afterwards, Auharmazd recited the Ahunavar thus: Yatha ahuv vairy ('as a heavenly lord is to be chosen'), &c. once, and uttered the twenty-one words; He also exhibited to the evil spirit His own triumph in the end, and the impotence of the evil spirit, the annihilation of the demons, and the resurrection and undisturbed future existence of the creatures for ever and everlasting. And the evil spirit, who perceived his own impotence and the annihilation of the demons, became confounded, and fell back to the gloomy darkness.

Auharmazd created his creatures in the confusion of Aharman; first he produced Vohuman ('good thought'), by whom the progress of the creatures of Auharmazd was advanced. Of Auharmazd's creatures of the world, the first was the sky; the second, water; the third, earth; the fourth, plants; the fifth, animals; the sixth, mankind.

title.en: Adapa and the Food of Life
title.zh: 阿達帕與生命之食

region.zh: 埃利都（伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian (Amarna copies, c. 14th c. BCE); trans. Rogers, 1912

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, trans. Robert W. Rogers, 'The Myth of Adapa'

summary.en: Adapa, son of Ea, breaks the wing of the south wind; Ea warns him that food and water of death will be set before him in heaven — but Anu offers food and water of LIFE instead, and Adapa, obeying Ea, refuses them, losing immortality for himself and all mankind.
summary.zh: 埃亞之子阿達帕折斷南風之翼；埃亞預警：天上必奉致死之食水，慎勿受——然安努所奉乃生命之食水，阿達帕遵師言而拒之，遂失永生，人類從此有死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Babylonian myth; presented as a comparative-mythology text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: O South wind, on the way I shall to thee [...] everything that, thy wing will I break. As he spoke with his mouth, the wing of the South wind was broken, seven days the South wind blew not upon the land. Anu called to his messenger Ilabrat: Why has the South wind not blown upon the land for seven days? His messenger Ilabrat answered him: "My lord, Adapa, the son of Ea, the wing of the South wind has broken."

Be astonished. Good words they will speak to Anu. A good countenance of Anu they will show thee. When thou standest before Anu, food of death they will set before thee, eat not. Water of death they will set before thee, drink not. Garments they will set before thee, put them on. Oil they will set before thee, anoint thyself. The counsel that I have given thee, forget not. The words which I have spoken, hold fast." The messenger of Anu came: "Adapa has broken the wing of the South wind. Bring him before me." The road to Heaven he made him take, and to Heaven he ascended.

"Bring him, that we may eat." Food of life they brought him, but he ate not. Water of life they brought him, but he drank not. Garments they brought him. He clothed himself. Oil they brought him. He anointed himself. Anu looked at him; he wondered at him. "Come, Adapa, why hast thou not eaten, not drunken? (Now) thou shalt not live. [...] Ea, my lord said: 'Eat not, drink not.' Take him and bring him back to his earth."

title.en: The Birth of Huitzilopochtli at Coatepec
title.zh: 維齊洛波奇特利誕於蛇山

region.zh: 蛇山（神話地：今墨西哥城一帶）

texts.period: Florentine Codex (Sahagun, c. 1578-80) and related codex traditions

source.work: H. H. Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III: Myths and Languages (1875), Aztec chapter (after Clavigero's version of the Sahagun tradition)

summary.en: Coatlicue, sweeping on the hill of Coatepec, conceives from a ball of humming-bird feathers; her daughter Coyolxauhqui rallies the four hundred stars to slay her, but at the moment of her death the young Huitzilopochtli springs from her womb in full war-gear, and with the fire-serpent he dismembers his sister and routs the stars of night.
summary.zh: 科阿特利庫埃於蛇山掃地，懷羽球而孕；其女科約爾沙赫吉聚四百星辰欲弒之。臨難之際，青年維齊洛波奇特利全副武裝自母腹躍出，持火蛇斬其姊，肢解其身，逐散夜之群星。

sensitivity.note: Aztec (Mexica) codical tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases referencing the Florentine Codex. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] While Coatlicue swept the temple hill of Coatepec, a ball of humming-bird feathers descended upon her, and she gathered it into her bosom; when she sought it again it was gone, and she had conceived a child. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui, shamed by the pregnancy, stirred the four hundred of the southern stars to slay their mother.

[Condensed paraphrase] At the moment the attackers reached the summit, Coatlicue gave birth to Huitzilopochtli, arrayed in shield, brand, and feather crest, with a face of blue stripes. He slew Coyolxauhqui with the fire-serpent, cut her pieces rolling down the hill, and put her mother's enemies to flight in all directions — and the mother's heart was made glad by her son.

title.en: The Storm-God and the Serpent Illuyanka
title.zh: 風雨神與蛇魔伊盧揚卡

region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

texts.period: Hittite tablet narratives (c. 14th-13th c. BCE), New Year ritual texts

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and ritual texts

summary.en: At the festival of the new year the Hittites recited how the serpent Illuyanka defeated the storm-god Tarhunna; the goddess Inara built a feast-house, lured the serpent and his children out with wine, and the storm-god — or, in the older telling, the son of the god and a mortal girl — slew the serpent while it was drunk.
summary.zh: 歲首祭典中，西臺人誦此神話：蛇魔伊盧揚卡擊敗風雨神塔爾渾那；女神伊娜拉築宴屋，以酒誘蛇及其子而出；風雨神——或古本中神與凡女所生之子——乘其醉而誅之。

[Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The serpent Illuyanka contended with the storm-god Tarhunna and overcame him; the god's heart and eyes the serpent took away. The goddess Inara built a house of feast on the sea-shore, filled it with wine, and called the serpent and his brood to eat and drink.

[Condensed paraphrase] They drank till their bellies were swollen and the pit was shut against them; then the storm-god — or, in the second telling, the son the god had by a mortal woman — came and killed the serpent while it was drunk. The festival of the purulli recited this victory each year, that the order of the land might be renewed with the spring.

title.en: Kumarbi and the Gods of the Stone
title.zh: 庫馬爾比與石中之神

region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

texts.period: Hittite tablet narratives (Song of Kumarbi, c. 14th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and texts

summary.en: The Hittite succession song: Alalu ruled, then Anu, whose feet Kumarbi bit off and swallowed as he pulled him from the sky — but the seed in his belly became the storm-god, and the stone Teshub was born of the mountain's side; the gods of the first ages fight their sons in a cycle older than the Greek story of Cronus.
summary.zh: 西臺王權交替之歌：阿拉魯在位，繼以阿努；庫馬爾比咬斷其足而吞之——腹中之種遂成風雨神，圖什普塔自山岩而生；太古諸神與其子相爭，此環早於希臘克洛諾斯之事。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In former times Alalu was king in heaven; Anu his cupbearer overcame him and reigned. But Anu in turn was fought by Kumarbi, who pulled the king of heaven down from the sky and bit off his genitals and swallowed them — and rejoiced, till he was told what he had swallowed.

[Condensed paraphrase] The seed of Anu grew in Kumarbi's belly and could not be brought forth; he spat out what became the stone of the mountain, and the storm-god Teshub was born, to fight Kumarbi for the kingship of heaven — a war of the old gods and the young that the Hittite singers put at the beginning of the world.

title.en: The Vanishing of Telipinu and the World's Withering
title.zh: 泰利皮努失蹤與世界枯槁

region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

texts.period: Hittite tablet narrative (Vanishing Deity myth, c. 14th-13th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite cult and ritual

summary.en: Telipinu the god of the fields walked away in anger, put on his black leather boots, and vanished — and at once the fog filled the windows, the hearths went out, sheep and cattle neglected their young, and the land lay barren; the god was called back with honey and oil and a great eagle, and in his return the fields and the hearths were filled again.
summary.zh: 田疇之神泰利皮努怒而去，足登黑皮靴，隱形不見——霧塞窗牖，爐火俱熄，羊牛棄其子，大地荒蕪。眾神以蜂蜜、膏油與巨鷹召之；神歸則田疇復茂，爐火復燃。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Telipinu the god of agriculture went away in anger; he put his right shoe on his left foot and his left on his right, and disappeared. Fog filled the windows of the houses, the fires went out in the hearths, the sheep and the cattle would not suckle their young, and in the land neither man nor god knew plenty.

[Condensed paraphrase] The sun-god sent the eagle to search the high mountains, and Kamrusepa the goddess of magic lulled the angry god with honey and oil and soft things; when Telipinu returned, the fires were relit, the flocks took their young, and the land was filled again — the ritual of return was acted out at Hattusa whenever the earth stood barren.

title.en: Lac Long Quan and Au Co: Dragon and Fairy
title.zh: 貉龍君與嫗姬：龍仙之種

region.en: Phu Tho / Red River delta, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南富壽／紅河三角洲

texts.period: Linh Nam chich quai, 14th-15th c. compilation of older legends

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'Hong-Lo the Giant'

summary.en: Lac Long Quan, the dragon-lord of the water country, slew the nine-tailed fox, the sea monster, and the wood demon of the northern borders; Au Co the mountain fairy came to him, and she laid a pouch of a hundred eggs — from which sprang a hundred sons, the ancestors of the hundred Viet clans; the dragon went back to the water, the fairy to the mountain, and the eldest ruled the Red River land as Hung Vuong.
summary.zh: 水國龍君貉龍誅九尾狐、海怪與北疆樹妖；山仙嫗姬來歸，產百卵之囊——化為百子，是為百越之祖。龍歸於水，仙歸於山，長子治紅河之地，是為涇陽王之後雄王。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese foundational legend from the Linh Nam chich quai; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lac Long Quan, the son of the water country, went about the lands killing the monsters of the early world: the nine-tailed fox of the western mountains, the sea-devil of the south, and the wood spirit that plagued the north; wherever he passed the people could live in peace, for he taught them to plant rice and to wear clothes.

[Condensed paraphrase] Au Co the fairy of the mountains came to dwell with him, and she bore a pouch of a hundred eggs, from which a hundred children hatched. Because a dragon must live in the water and a fairy on the mountain, they divided the children: fifty went with their mother to the hills, fifty with their father to the sea-lands, and the eldest was made the first Hung king of the Red River country.

title.en: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh: The Mountain and the Water
title.zh: 山精與水精：山與水之爭

region.en: Ba Vi mountains, Red River, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南巴維山與紅河

texts.period: Vietnamese folk legend (Linh Nam chich quai traditions)

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'The Rival Genii'

summary.en: Both the mountain spirit and the water spirit sought the eighteenth daughter of the Hung king; the king set a trial — gifts first brought wins — and Son Tinh, whose presents were there at dawn, won the bride. Thuy Tinh raised the flood with whirlwinds and storms against the mountain, but the mountain rose the higher; each year the waters come and fall again, which men call the monsoon.
summary.zh: 山精與水精同求雄王之十八女；王設試禮——先至者得娶。山精黎明而達，遂成婚。水精怒，興風作浪、引洪灌山，而山愈漲愈高；水年年復來復去——人謂之季風雨季。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese folk legend of the Hung kings' age; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the Hung king sought a husband for My Nuong his eighteenth daughter, two spirits came to woo her in one day: Son Tinh, lord of the mountains, and Thuy Tinh, lord of the waters. The king said the one whose presents came first should have her; at dawn the mountain spirit's gifts of stone and timber were already before the hall, and the marriage was made.

[Condensed paraphrase] Thuy Tinh returned in fury with the waters: he raised storms and floods against the mountain where the couple dwelt, and the people of the plain suffered year by year; but the mountain lifted itself the higher, and the waters sank each time — the war never ends, and the yearly rise and fall of the water is the struggle still remembered.

title.en: Thanh Giong Rides to Phu Dong
title.zh: 扶董天王聖郎

region.en: Phu Dong village, Bac Ninh (Hanoi region), Vietnam
region.zh: 越南北寧扶董村

texts.period: Vietnamese legend (Viet dien u linh tap, 13th-14th c. compilation)

source.work: Gustave Dumoutier, Legendes historiques de l'Annam et du Tonkin (Hanoi: F.-H. Schneider, 1887) - the Phu-Dong legend

summary.en: A boy of Phu Dong village, three years old and mute, sat up at the king's call for warriors and spoke his first words: the horse and the iron rod would fight the invaders; he ate the village's rice and grew instantly a giant, took the iron rod and the iron horse, put the enemy to flight with fire from the horse's mouth, and rode up the mountain alone — the tutelary god of the village to this day.
summary.zh: 扶董村三歲不言童子，聞王募武士而起，忽發初聲：「鐵馬鐵鞭，必退敵！」食一村之飯，頃刻成巨人；執鐵鞭、乘鐵馬，馬口噴火破敵——遂獨上羅浮山而去，鄉人立祠奉為本境城隍。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese hero myth from the Viet dien u linh tap; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the armies of the north invaded the land of the Hung kings, the king sent out the call for warriors; in Phu Dong village a boy of three, who had never spoken, sat up in his mother's arms and answered the call in words, asking that a horse and a rod of iron be sent.

[Condensed paraphrase] He ate what the village cooked and grew from child to man in a day; when the enemy came he mounted the iron horse, which breathed fire, and broke them with the iron rod until their armor rang like rain. At the bounds of So'n mountain he rode up alone into the sky, and the king gave him the title Heavenly King of Phu Dong — the village god who is honored still when the spring festival goes round.

title.en: The Vision of Arda Viraf: Bridge, Damsel, and Hell
title.zh: 阿爾達·維拉夫之異象：橋、少女與地獄

region.en: Fars, Sasanian Persia (vision of the spirit realm)
region.zh: 薩珊波斯法爾斯（靈界異象）

texts.period: Arda Viraf Namak, Sasanian-era Pahlavi text; trans. Haug (with West), 1872

source.work: The Book of Arda Viraf, trans. Martin Haug (1872), chs. 4-5, 17-18

summary.en: The Zoroastrian Dante four centuries before Dante: chosen by lot after a council of the priests, Viraf drinks the narcotic of Vishtasp and his soul crosses the Chinwad bridge — where his own religion and deeds meet him 'in the graceful form of a damsel' — beholds the reward of the pious in Garothman and the many torments of hell, and returns to report truly.
summary.zh: 早但丁四百年之祆教《神曲》：祭司議會抽籤選中維拉夫，飲維什塔斯普之迷藥，其靈魂渡欽瓦特橋——其宗教與善行化為「婀娜少女」相迎——得見伽羅斯曼中義人之報與地獄諸刑，歸而如實稟告。

sensitivity.note: Zoroastrian religious vision literature of great influence on Parsi devotion (and famously compared with Dante); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Taking the first footstep with the good thought, and the second footstep with the good word, and the third footstep with the good deed, I came up to the Chinwad bridge, the very wide and strong and created by Ohrmazd. [...] And there stood before him his own religion and his own deeds, in the graceful form of a damsel, as a beautiful appearance [...] And the soul of the pious asked that damsel thus: 'Who art thou? [...] To him replied she who was his own religion and his own deeds, thus: 'I am thy actions, O youth of good thoughts, of good words, of good deeds, of good religion. It is on account of thy will and actions that I am as great and good and sweet-scented and triumphant and undistressed as appears to thee.

And afterward, Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, took hold of my hand, so that I went on unhurt. In that manner, I beheld cold and heat, drought and stench, to such a degree as I never saw, nor heard of, in the world. And when I went farther, I also saw the greedy jaws of hell, like the most frightful pit, descending in a very narrow and fearful place; in darkness so gloomy that it is necessary to hold by the hand [...] and when three days and nights have elapsed he says thus: 'The nine thousand years are completed, and they will not release me!'

And I saw the darkest hell, which is pernicious, dreadful, terrible, very painful, mischievous and foul-smelling. And after further observation, it appeared to me as a pit, to the bottom of which, a thousand cubits would not reach [...] and as many as the hairs on the mane of a horse, so close and many in number, the souls of the wicked stand, but they see not and hear no sound, one from the other; everyone thinks thus: 'I am alone'.

title.en: The Chinvat Bridge Judgment
title.zh: 欽瓦特橋的審判

region.en: Persia (symbolic: the unseen world beyond the bridge)
region.zh: 波斯（象徵：橋彼岸之幽冥世界）

texts.period: Avestan c. 1000-600 BCE, Pahlavi accounts 8th-9th c. CE; Dhalla ed. 1914

source.work: M. N. Dhalla, 'Zoroastrian Theology' (1914), ch. XIX 'Death and Beyond'

summary.en: In Zoroastrian teaching the soul lingers three days and nights beside the corpse, then journeys to the unseen world, where its own conscience appears as a beautiful maiden (for the good) or a taunting hag (for the wicked). Every soul must cross the Chinvat Bridge of Judgment: the righteous pass with spirit-guard dogs' help into a four-tiered heaven, while the wicked fall into a four-tiered hell of poisonous food and endless darkness.
summary.zh: 瑣羅亞斯德教認為，亡魂死後三晝夜停留屍旁，隨即啟程前往幽冥之境：義人的良心化身絕美少女相迎，惡人則受醜嫗嘲弄。一切靈魂皆須渡過審判之橋——欽瓦特橋：義人得靈犬相助進入四重天國，惡人則墮入以毒物為食、黑暗無底的四層地獄。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed, fully paraphrased retellings of Dhalla's chapter XIX in the collector's own words. Source caveat: the planned primary source (SBE Vol. 5, 'Pahlavi Texts Part I', tr. E. W. West, 1880) was inaccessible (sacred-texts.com returns 403), so Dhalla's 1914 PD scholarly synthesis was substituted; it is secondary, so exact Pahlavi chapter attributions are less precise. Category 'religious': scriptural/doctrinal eschatology rather than folk narrative. Coordinates are symbolic — the Chinvat Bridge is an otherworldly location, placed inland at Yazd, a historic centre of surviving Zoroastrianism.

passages.text: In Zoroastrian thought, death is a trial no one escapes: even legendary heroes like Yima fell to Astovidhotu, the demon of death. After the body dies, the soul remains near it for three days and nights, retracing the deeds of its lifetime. The soul of a righteous person sits by the spot where the head once rested, chanting sacred hymns and feeling joy as great as all the living world combined, while the soul of a wicked person sits near the skull in bewildered dread and suffering as great as all the living world combined. At the fourth dawn the journey into the unseen world begins. The righteous soul travels amid a sweet south wind, and then meets its own daena — religious conscience appearing as a damsel of unmatched beauty — who reveals that she is simply the embodiment of its own good thoughts, words, and deeds. Helpers such as Sraosha and Rashnu escort such a soul on its way. The wicked walk a dreadful path in a foul north wind and, in the Pahlavi accounts, are confronted by their conscience in the shape of an ugly old hag mocking the wicked life they led.

Every soul, good or bad, must pass over the Chinvat Bridge before entering the world beyond, for it stands as the crossing point of judgment. Spirit hounds are stationed at the bridge; they lend aid to devout souls, while the wicked find none. Whoever recites the Ahuna Vairya prayer in full faith is enabled by Ahura Mazda to cross and reach the best existence, the best righteousness, and the best lights; a true priest is one whose wise teaching leaves a person easy of conscience at the bridge, whereas anyone who mistreats dogs in life finds the way barred. Paradise has four levels — Good Thought, Good Word, Good Deed, and highest of all Garonmana, the abode of endless light — where the archangel Vohu Manah greets the newcomers and celestial food, embroidered robes, and golden thrones are provided. Hell likewise has four depths, ending in endless, stinking darkness, where Angra Mainyu feeds souls the foulest food amid the mockery of the infernal rabble.

title.en: The Epic of Gilgamesh: King, Friend, and Seeker of Immortality
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什史詩：王者、摯友與不死者之追尋

region.zh: 南伊拉克烏魯克

texts.period: Standard Babylonian recension (Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 13th-11th c. BCE, copied from Old Babylonian forerunners (c. 19th-17th c. BCE); principal mss: Nineveh/Kuyunjik library tablets (British Museum K-series), e.g. K 3375 = Tablet XI; Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet

source.archive: Oxford (critical edition: Andrew George) / ETCSL (Sumerian poems)
source.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh, trans. Andrew George (Penguin, 1999); Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature for the Sumerian Bilgames poems

texts.license: Sumerian corpus translation (ETCSL) open access; Penguin translation quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The tyrant king Gilgamesh and the wild man Enkidu become friends, kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, and are punished by Enkidu's death; Gilgamesh crosses the world to Utnapishtim, fails the sleep test, loses the plant of youth to a serpent, and returns to carve his story on the walls of Uruk — death keeps even heroes, but the city remembers.
summary.zh: 暴君吉爾伽美什與野人恩奇都結為摯友，共誅洪巴巴與天牛，卻因觸怒諸神而摯友亡故；吉爾伽美什橫越天際尋求不死，未通睡眠之試，青春之草又為蛇所竊；返鄉於烏魯克城垣刻其事——英雄終有一死，而城郭銘記其名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (K 3375): Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how Ea warned him through the wall of a reed hut to tear down his house and build a ship; he sealed the boat, loaded the seed of all living, and the storm destroyed the land for seven days; the raven, sent last and not returning, showed him the receding waters. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (K 3375); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (end): Utnapishtim says, 'Death is the lot decreed for all: no one has ever seen the face of death, yet no one has ever escaped it.' Gilgamesh, woken after six days and seven nights of sleep he believed were minutes, fails the test; a serpent smells the plant of youth as he bathes, seizes it, and sloughs its skin — and Gilgamesh weeps. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet XI (end); not verbatim.

texts.language: Akkadian (Standard Babylonian; Old Babylonian forerunners; Sumerian sources)
texts.canonical_translation: Andrew George, The Epic of Gilgamesh, Penguin Classics, 1999 (critical edition: Andrew George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford, 2003)

narrative.en:
The Standard Babylonian epic assembles in twelve tablets a two-thousand-year-old literary history. It opens with a prologue inviting the reader to climb the walls of Uruk: 'See its foundation terrace, touch the masonry — is it not burnt brick and good? ... One league city, one league palm gardens, one league lowlands, the open area of the Ishtar Temple...' — and to read the box of lapis within, the story of 'him who saw the Deep' (sa naqba imuru), Gilgamesh, two-thirds god, one-third human, whom no one could equal.

ENKIDU. Gilgamesh, shepherd-king of Uruk, works his young men at the game-stick and exhausts the brides with his custom (the ius primae noctis in the Old Babylonian text). The people cry to heaven; Aruru pinches off a rival in the clay of the steppe: Enkidu, shaggy with hair like grain, who eats grass with gazelles and drinks at the water-holes, blocking the hunters' traps. A harlot (Shamhat) is sent to tame him: seven days of love-making 'after the manner of mankind' leave the gazelles shunning him; she clothes him, feeds him bread and beer, gives him shepherds' work, and news of Gilgamesh's wedding custom. Enkidu goes to Uruk to meet him at the wedding door; they wrestle furiously in the street — doorposts quake, the wall shakes — and Enkidu, defeated, embraces the king, and the two become fast friends.

THE CEDAR FOREST. Gilgamesh resolves to journey to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian Humbaba, whose mouths are fire, whose breath is death, whom Enlil appointed to terrify men. The elders of Uruk counsel against it; Enkidu recalls he has seen the forest and knows its horror. Gilgamesh has doors made for Enlil from cedar and entreats Shamash for aid; Shamash promises eight winds behind him. They cross seven mountain ranges, and Enkidu, seized by dreams three times, keeps waking Gilgamesh: while he sleeps, Humbaba hears them and batters down the mountains. Shamash raises the winds — thirteen, like whips — and Humbaba, bound and helpless, offers surrender ('I will be your slave, my forest is yours'). Enkidu insists on killing him: 'Where is your strength of courage?' The guardian's head is severed and bagged; on the return Enkidu's broken door is dedicated to Enlil.

ISHTAR AND THE BULL. Back in Uruk, Ishtar offers herself in marriage; Gilgamesh refuses with the famous catalogue of her ruined lovers — the bird, the lion, the horse, the shepherd, the plant Tammuz — 'you are a brazier which goes out in the cold'. Enraged, Ishtar demands the Bull of Heaven from Anu; refused at first, then granted at threat of breaking the underworld doors. The Bull snorts a pit (one hundred men fall in), then another; Enkidu seizes its tail, Gilgamesh stabs it between neck and horns, and they dedicate its heart to Shamash while Ishtar curses from the wall. Enkidu hurls the right thigh at her. That night the gods deliberate: for killing Humbaba and the Bull, one of the two must die. Enkidu falls sick for twelve days, cursing first the door, then the harlot (who taught him mankind's ways), and blessing her after she is counseled back; he dreams of the House of Dust, where thrones are dust and Belit-Seri keeps the house, and where he sits for ever with kings and priests — and dies.

THE JOURNEY TO UTNAPISHTIM. Gilgamesh's grief is wild: he weeps six days and nights 'as a lioness', roams the steppe clothed in a lion's skin, resolves to go to Utnapishtim 'the Faraway', who escaped the flood, and ask the secret of life. He passes the twin peaks of Mashu whose gates guard the sun's path, and walks a dark league-road twelve leagues deep 'where there is neither light nor dark'; at a garden of jewel-trees he meets the alewife Siduri, who (in the older Old Babylonian telling, abbreviated in the Standard version) counsels feasting and love — 'when the gods made mankind they set death apart for mankind' — then directs him to the ferryman Urshanabi, who asks for the 'stone things'; Gilgamesh smashes them, and must cut wooden punts, kissing each pole before use to cross the Waters of Death.

THE FLOOD AND THE TEST. Utnapishtim tells him the secret the gods swore and Ea leaked through the reed hut's wall: 'Tear down the house, build a ship; leave possessions, save life'. The boat is a cube, 120 cubits a side, sealed with pitch and bitumen, loaded with gold, silver, cattle, beasts, craftsmen, and the seed of all living. The storm: 'the gods were frightened by the flood... the goddess wailed like a woman in childbirth'; after seven days the ship grounded on Nisir, and the birds went out — dove, swallow, raven (the raven did not return). Enlil, furious that a man survived, is appeased by Ea, who argues he should have sent plague, famine — not flood — and Enlil blesses Utnapishtim and his wife, making them like gods, to dwell 'at the mouth of the rivers'. Now the test: sleep six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh dozes at once; his wife bakes a loaf each day, and when he wakes he sees the bread's stages and knows he slept — 'death is the decree, the word of the assembly'. Utnapishtim sends him back; as a parting gift, the plant of youth (like a boxthorn, 'an old man will turn young'); on the homeward road Gilgamesh bathes in a pool, and a serpent smells the plant, seizes it, sloughs its skin, and vanishes. Gilgamesh weeps and returns to Uruk; the epic ends where it began, with the city walls. (Tablet 12, appended in the Nineveh library, translates a separate Sumerian poem in which Enkidu descends to retrieve Gilgamesh's ball and drum, is trapped, and his shade rises to describe the netherworld — a scribal appendix, not part of the main plot.)

FUNCTIONS. The epic is the masterpiece of Mesopotamian wisdom literature: it critiques despotic kingship, mourns friendship, and sets human fame (the city's walls) against death; it served as school text and royal library copy (Ashurbanipal's collection); the flood episode fed Mesopotamian historiography and, via Berossus, into later comparative debate.
narrative.zh: 史詩始於烏魯克城垣之邀：觀其磚基，讀青金石匣中『見過深淵者』吉爾伽美什之事。野人恩奇都為母神所造，與神妓七日交好而開化；赴烏魯克與王角力，不敵而結為友。二人西赴雪松林誅洪巴巴，返城後吉爾伽美什拒伊什塔爾之婚，殺天牛、擲其腿；諸神議定二者取一，恩奇都病十二日，夢『塵土之家』而死。王披獅皮漫遊，越馬什雙峰、經酒肆西杜里之諭，與擺渡人烏爾沙那比渡死水；不死者烏特那皮什提告以洪水之秘：蘆牆內聞以利亞之諭，造方舟、納生靈、七日暴風、放鴉知地。又試以七日不眠而王立酣，麵包示時；遂返。臨別得青春之草，浴時為蛇竊去蛻皮而遁。王泣而歸，於烏魯克城垣自述其事。第十二板為蘇美譯文附編，述恩奇都冥府之行。全篇批判暴政、悼友、以城記勝死，為美索不達米亞智慧文學之巔。

functions: Wisdom-literature meditation on mortality and the limits of kingship
Scribal curriculum text and royal library classic (Nineveh, Ashurbanipal)
Aition of Uruk's walls and of the hero's fame against death
Vessel for the Mesopotamian flood narrative (Tablet XI) in later traditions

variants.name: Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet ('Surpassing all kings')
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian, c. 18th-17th c. BCE (Univ. of Pennsylvania Museum)
variants.summary: Opens with the meeting of Gilgamesh and Enkidu (incomplete: the middle is lost) and preserves the fuller wedding-custom and wrestling scene; the lacuna is bridged by scholarly restoration from context.

variants.name: Old Babylonian Yale tablet (Siduri's counsel)
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian, c. 18th-17th c. BCE (Yale Babylonian Collection)
variants.summary: Preserves the tavern-keeper's carpe diem speech almost whole ('when the gods created mankind, death they allotted to mankind'); in the Standard Babylonian recension the speech is reduced to a mention — the older text is our main witness.

variants.name: Sumerian poems of Bilgames
variants.text_tradition: Sumerian narratives c. 21st-17th c. BCE (Nippur copies; ETCSL 1.8.x)
variants.summary: Five independent poems — Bilgames and Huwawa; Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld; The Death of Bilgames; etc. — in which Enkidu is the servant, Huwawa's killing is sacrilege, and death is met with wisdom; the Standard Babylonian epic reworks them into one arc.

variants.name: Hittite and Hurrian adaptations
variants.text_tradition: Bogazkoy tablets, c. 14th-13th c. BCE (fragmentary)
variants.summary: A Hittite adaptation (and Hurrian intermediaries) attests the epic's westward spread; heavily fragmentary — the narrative depends on reconstructed joining of scattered pieces (George 2003, vol. 2).

title.en: Atrahasis: The Making of Humanity and the Great Flood
title.zh: 阿特拉哈西斯：人類之造與大洪水

region.en: Nippur / Sippar region, Iraq (tablet findspots; symbolic pin at Nippur)
region.zh: 伊拉克尼普爾／西帕爾地區（泥板出土地；象徵性定位於尼普爾）

summary.en: The lesser gods, worn out digging rivers for the great gods, revolt; the wise Ea proposes the creation of humanity from clay mixed with a slain god's flesh to carry the labor. When humanity's noise disturbs Enlil, plague, drought, and finally flood are sent; Atrahasis is warned and saved, and the gods settle on regulated fertility rather than extinction.
summary.zh: 小神為大神疏河役苦，罷工圍宮；埃亞獻策，以死者之肉血摻黏土造人代役。人丁繁盛、喧聲擾恩利爾，遂遣疫、旱，終降洪水；阿特拉哈西斯奉諭造舟得存，諸神末以管制生育之策定約。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet I: the Igigi gods, having borne the gods' burden for 3,600 years, burn their tools and besiege Ellil's temple; Ea, called to counsel, proposes: let one god be slain, and the birth-goddess Nintu mix his flesh and blood with clay, so that a lullu — a human — is made to bear the toil of the gods. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet III: Enlil's flood sweeps the land for seven days and nights; Atrahasis, forewarned by Ea through the wall of his reed hut, has sealed the boat and brought the seed of living things; when Enlil discovers the survivor, Ea defends the deed, and Enlil touches the boat and blesses the pair. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tablet III; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: WHEN THE GODS WERE MEN. The poem opens 'enuma ilu awilum' — 'when the gods, instead of men, bore the work and suffered the toil': the great gods (Anu, Enlil, Enki) allotted offices while the lesser Igigi dug the Tigris and Euphrates, heaped basket-loads, and endured 'excessive toil' for 3,600 years. The gods' burden in those days is the poem's first premise: heaven's society was already a labor economy.

THE STRIKE AND THE MAKING OF MAN. The Igigi finally burn their tools, and in the night surround the dwelling of Ellil (Enlil), the executive god: 'Come, let us meet the vizier, that he may save us from our heavy toil'. Enlil, alarmed, calls the assembly; Anu counsels appeasement, and the wise Ea (Enki) proposes the solution: let one of the rebels — the god We-ila, who has the spirit/understanding — be slain, and let the birth-goddess Nintu (Mami) mix his flesh and blood with clay. She does so, stamping out lullu-people, and the first human is created 'to bear the service of god and man'. The gods, freed of labor, weep for joy and praise the birth-goddess ('Nintu, lady of all created things'); she is named 'Mistress of All the Gods', and in a closing ritual frame the poem remarks that the mixed god-flesh and human are 'enclosed' — three quarters human, one quarter god — the theological anthropology of Mesopotamia.

THE NOISE. For 1,200 years the land is populous and noisy; 'their cry disturbed the god, their uproar disturbed Ellil' (ribaba — the babel of mouths). Enlil resolves to reduce humanity, first by plague (Namtar sent); Atrahasis, 'very wise' (ra'is napišti — the name means 'exceedingly wise', also 'he of the far-drawn life'), is counseled by Ea: the god of plague must be worshiped, and the people must stop calling on their own gods and honor Namtar alone — the plague abates. Then drought: Adad withholds rain; again Ea instructs Atrahasis to redirect worship to Adad — rain returns. A third escalation ('the famine was severe') fails likewise.

THE FLOOD. Enlil finally persuades the assembly to send the deluge and swears them to secrecy — but Ea, sworn and unable to tell Atrahasis directly, speaks to the wall of Atrahasis' reed hut with Atrahasis listening: 'Wall, hear me; reed-wall, understand all my words: Dismantle your house, build a boat... save life against the destruction of the seed of mankind'. The boat is sealed with pitch, loaded with cattle, 'beasts and birds', and Atrahasis' family. The flood: 'Adad roared in the clouds... the flood was seven days and seven nights'. Nintu/Mami 'cried out like a woman in childbirth', lamenting her creation swallowed in the sea; the gods sit weeping on the heaven's rim, 'gathered like flies over the offering' (the Gilgamesh XI version of this line). When the waters subside, Atrahasis offers sacrifice on the mountain peak; Enlil, smelling it, 'plucked at his garment and ascended to heaven', furious that a survivor exists; Ea defends the deed ('you who are wise erred by sending the flood'), and Enlil descends, boards the boat, and blesses Atrahasis and his wife: 'Atrahasis, you shall be called 'Exceedingly Wise'... he shall dwell at the mouth of the rivers' — immortality in the far-away.

END: THE COMPROMISE. The poem's final section (much restored) sets the new world-order: instead of another flood, Enlil institutes population control through Nintu. Certain women ('the Ugbabtu, the Enu, and the Entu' — priestess classes) shall not bear children; the pasittu demon shall snatch the baby from the mother's lap; and classes of women are exempted from childbearing while some infants die — the theology of infant mortality and 'barren' office. Creation's labor problem is solved forever by regulated fertility, not extinction.

FUNCTIONS. Atrahasis is Mesopotamia's primeval-history epic: it aitiologizes human labor as the gods' relief, death's bite as demographic regulation, and ritual worship as the life-line of civilization; it is the direct source-text for Gilgamesh Tablet XI's flood, and through that channel (and Berossus) the ancestor-comparandum of all Near Eastern flood literature.
narrative.zh: 『當諸神尚如人類，負擔苦役』：伊吉吉挖河背土三千六百年，終焚工具圍困恩利爾。埃亞獻策誅韋伊拉，以其肉血摻黏土，生母寧圖捏成人形，名『盧魯』，代人負神役；諸神釋負歡呼。人丁繁盛一千二百年，喧聲擾恩利爾，遂遣疫癘、乾旱屢次；智者阿特拉哈西斯依埃亞之諭調整祭祀，瘟疫旱災皆退。恩利爾終遣洪水並令眾神守密；埃亞隔蘆牆傳諭：拆屋造舟、封以瀝青、納牲畜生靈。風暴七日，生母寧圖如產婦哀號，諸神聚泣如蠅。水退舟擱山巔，阿特拉哈西斯獻祭；恩利爾怒其倖存，埃亞抗辯，恩利爾登舟祝福：名之『極智者』，使居河口，得不死。末段記恩利爾立生育管制：設不產之女祭司，縱帕西圖魔奪嬰——以管轄人口代滅絕。全篇釋人類勞役、死之由、與祭祀之功能，並為吉爾伽美什第十一板洪水之源。

functions: Primeval history: anthropology of labor (humans created to relieve the gods)
Theodicy of infant mortality and priestess classes as demographic theology
Source text for the Gilgamesh flood and later Near Eastern flood literature
Ritual theology of worship as the mechanism that stays plague and drought

title.en: The Bundahishn: Ohrmazd's Creation and Ahriman's Assault
title.zh: 《創世紀》：阿胡拉·馬茲達創世與阿赫里曼之侵

region.en: Sasanian Persia (symbolic pin at Fars province)
region.zh: 薩珊波斯（象徵性定位於法爾斯省）

texts.period: Pahlavi cosmological compendium, Sasanian strata c. 4th-6th c. CE, copied 9th-11th c.; principal MS: Indian Bundahishn (Bombay) and Iranian Bundahishn (Copenhagen MS)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (West, SBE vol. 5, 1880)
source.work: Bundahishn chs. 1-4, 34 (Pahlavi); trans. E. W. West, Pahlavi Texts Part I, Sacred Books of the East vol. 5, Oxford 1880

summary.en: Ohrmazd creates the good creation in six stages — sky, water, earth, plants, animals, man (Gayomart) — and the seven Amesha Spentas; Ahriman bursts up from the darkness to destroy it; Ohrmazd recites the Ahuna Vairya, drives him back, and seals the attack for nine thousand years, fixing history as a battle the good creation will win.
summary.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達以六段造善世——天、水、地、植物、動物、原人伽約馬特——並七大天使；阿赫里曼自黑暗突起毀世；馬茲達誦阿胡納·瓦里亞經文擊退之，封其侵擾九千年——歷史遂為善必勝之戰。

sensitivity.note: Scripture of a living tradition (Zoroastrian/Parsi); the Yasna liturgy is sacred and is not reproduced; Bundahishn cosmology is a public Pahlavi text.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 1 (West 1880): 'Ohrmazd is in the light on high, Ahriman in the abyss of darkness below... both are limited and unlimited... between them is the void, in which their meeting shall occur.' Ohrmazd creates the creation spiritually first, then materially, in six stages. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 1 (West 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 3-4: Ohrmazd recites the Ahuna Vairya prayer, twenty-one words matching the twenty-one books of the scripture; Ahriman, seeing the creation, is confounded, and for three thousand years lies fettered; he then bursts up through the earth's middle and defiles the waters, the earth, the fire, and the plants; Gayomart and the unique ox are slain — from the ox's body spring the plants and animals, from Gayomart's body the first human couple. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 3-4; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Bundahishn ('Primal Creation') is the Zoroastrian book of cosmogony, cosmology, and apocalypse — a Sasanian-era Pahlavi compendium preserving a theology whose oldest layers are the Gathas of Zarathustra.

BEGINNING: THE TWO SPIRITS. Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda) dwells in endless light on high; Ahriman (Angra Mainyu) in the abyss of darkness below; between them stretches the void in which they will meet. Ohrmazd 'is in knowledge, goodness, and light'; Ahriman in 'stinging venom and darkness' — and their knowledge runs backward and forward nine thousand years. Ohrmazd creates first spiritually (menog, the 'thought-state'): the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, and man — six creations in six stages, each guarded by one of the seven Amesha Spentas (Vohu Manah, Asha Vahishta, Khshathra Vairya, Spenta Armaiti, Haurvatat, Ameretat, with Ohrmazd/Spena? as the seventh) — then materially (getig), clothing each creation in body. The cosmology is numerically ordered: 3,000 years of spiritual creation; Ahriman bound; the final 3,000 years of the mixed state; and the last 3,000 under the Saviors.

MIDDLE: THE ASSAULT. Ahriman, seeing the good creation in the light, is confounded by its perfection and by Ohrmazd's recitation of the Ahuna Vairya — twenty-one words whose power binds him; he lies fettered for three thousand years. Then, roused by the spirit Jeh (the whore-demon), he rises, bursting up through the middle of the earth: he defiles the water with salt, corrupts the fire with smoke, sows noxious creatures (khrafstra) in the plants, and brings disease, decay, and death into the animals. He reaches up to the sky's dome and enters creation through it; the sky is cracked, and the battle of history begins. Gayomart, the primal man, and the unique ox (Gopatshah? the Uniquely-created Ox) are slain by Ahriman's assault — but their deaths are productive: from the ox's body spring fifty-five kinds of grain and twelve kinds of medicinal plants, and from its seed, purified in the moon, the pairs of animals; from Gayomart's body, purified in the sun, grows the rivas plant from which Mashya and Mashyana, the first human couple, arise. Death itself is thus revealed as transformed fertility: the assault of evil becomes the field of its own defeat.

END: THE SEALED BATTLE. Ohrmazd binds the assault: 'the creatures of Ahriman... he placed in the earth' — and Ahriman is sealed back through the hole by which he came, while Ohrmazd sets the celestial spheres in motion — 12,000 years apportioned among the four ages, with the sun's path, the stars' stations (the 6,488? the fixed and wandering stars), and the mountains as fortresses (the earth's mountains are 'the garners' that hold back the waters). Time is now the arena: history runs as a battle in which every act of righteousness (asha) strengthens the good creation and every sin feeds Ahriman, until the final renovation (Frashokereti — Bundahishn 34, cross-referenced).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Zoroastrian dualist ethics (every deed affects the cosmic battle), the ritual duties (protecting the good creations — water, fire, earth, cattle — from pollution), the priestly calendar (the 12,000-year scheme and the Saviors), and the eschatology of the molten river; it is recited and taught in Parsi and Irani communities, and its imagery structured Sasanian royal art (the rock reliefs of the investiture).
narrative.zh: 《創世紀》（班達希申）開篇：奧爾馬茲德居高處光明中，阿赫里曼居下界黑暗深淵，其間為鴻溝；二者皆知前後九千年之事。馬茲達先以『默界』（menog）創造六段——天、水、地、植物、動物、原人——由七大天使各守其一，後賦以『實界』（getig）之體。阿赫里曼見善世完美而懼，為阿胡納·瓦里亞二十一字所縛，囚三千年；後經女魔耶赫所激，破地而出：使水鹹、火生煙、於植物中播毒蟲，以病老死入獸界；原人伽約馬特與獨牛被殺——然牛身出五十五種穀物與十二種藥草，牛種經月淨而生百獸之偶；伽約馬特之身經日淨而生瑞瓦斯植物，從中生初人夫婦馬希亞與馬希亞娜。馬茲達封閉邪侵之路，立天球之運行，分歷史為四紀一萬二千年：善惡之戰即歷史，凡義行皆壯善世，凡罪皆飼惡靈，直至末世淨化之河。功能：善惡二元倫理、護善四物之祭儀、祭司曆法、以及薩珊王家藝術之意象。

title.en: The Song of Ullikummi: Kumarbi's Stone Giant and the Storm-god's War
title.zh: 烏利庫米之歌：庫馬爾比之石巨與風暴神之戰

region.zh: 土耳其哈圖沙（博阿茲柯伊；泥板出土地）

texts.period: Tablets c. 14th-13th c. BCE (Hittite copies of Hurrian material); principal tablets from Bogazkoy (Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin; Istanbul Archaeological Museums)

source.work: Song of Ullikummi (Kumarbi Cycle, CTH 345), trans. Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths, Atlanta 1998

texts.license: Cuneiform text public domain; Hoffner 1998 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Deposed by the storm-god Teshub, Kumarbi mates with a great rock cliff and fathers the stone giant Ullikummi, who grows deaf and blind on the shoulder of the sleeping giant Upelluri; Teshub's weapons fail, the wise Ea finds the ancient reed-knife that first separated heaven and earth and cuts the giant loose, and the final battle is fought — the tablet breaks at the climax.
summary.zh: 庫馬爾比遭風暴神特舒卜廢黜，遂與巨巖交合，生石巨人烏利庫米，託沉睡巨人烏佩魯里肩上生長，聾且盲；特舒卜兵刃不能傷；智神埃亞尋得上古分天地之銅刀，斷巨人足而解放之；決戰將分勝負之際，泥板斷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; Hittite cultural heritage (Turkey).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 i-ii: Kumarbi 'took his seat and his mind plotted a battle: he set his right hand on the rock and his left foot on it... and fathered on the rock a terrible stone'; the midwives lift the newborn, and Kumarbi exults: 'I have created a rival for Teshub... his name shall be Ullikummi.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 i-ii; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 iv: Ea descends to Upelluri, who groans: 'When heaven and earth were built upon me, I knew nothing; now something small pains my right shoulder.' Ea finds the old reed-knife with which heaven and earth were once cut apart, and with it severs Ullikummi's feet from Upelluri's shoulder. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 iv; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths, Writings from the Ancient World 2, Atlanta 1998 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Song of Ullikummi is the masterpiece of the Kumarbi Cycle — the Hittite succession mythology (CTH 344-345) whose castration-scheme parallels Hesiod's Theogony and whose war in heaven foreshadows Greek Titanomachy imagery.

BEGINNING: THE DEPOSED KING'S PLOT. The Song opens in the tradition of the Song of Kumarbi (CTH 344): the old king Kumarbi, deposed by the storm-god Teshub, 'took his seat and his mind plotted battle'. He goes to the great rock cliff of Urkis by the sea, sets his right hand and left foot upon it, and impregnates the stone; the midwife-goddesses deliver a stone child, and Kumarbi exults: 'I have created a rival for Teshub... let his name be Ullikummi.' He sends the child — deaf, blind, made of diorite — far away to the shoulder of the sleeping giant Upelluri, the Atlas-figure 'on whose shoulders heaven and earth are built', to grow in secret; the messenger warns: 'when he is grown, he will be like a god'.

MIDDLE: THE GIANT RISES. The sun-god, circling the heavens, sees a strange new height rising from the sea and reports to Teshub; the storm-god ascends Mount Hazzi with his brothers and looks: a stone tower is growing on Upelluri's shoulder, already taller than Hazzi and his brother Namni. Teshub's first assault fails: his thunder and lightning cannot split the stone, his heart 'melts like lead'; the goddess Ishtar sings to charm the giant — deaf as stone, he does not hear. Teshub's consort Hebat panics; the giant is growing to besiege the city Kummiya. The wise Ea is called from his sea-house; he descends to Upelluri and asks: 'do you know why your right shoulder pains you?' The sleeping giant groans: 'when heaven and earth were built upon me, I knew nothing; now something small has begun to pain me.' Ea recognizes Ullikummi and descends into the old storehouse of the gods, where he finds the ancient copper reed-knife 'with which heaven and earth were once cut apart' — the primal instrument of separation.

END: THE CUTTING AND THE FINAL BATTLE. Ea severs Ullikummi's feet from Upelluri's shoulder with the reed-knife: the giant, cut loose from his foundation, still stands — but is now mortal-sized and can be fought. Ea's sons carry word to Teshub: 'go and fight, and let the gods watch you'. The storm-god mounts his chariot, storms gather behind him, and he confronts the deaf giant in single combat — 'Teshub drove Ullikummi into the sea? he hurled him into the sea' — and the tablet breaks at the climax. The fragments suggest Teshub's victory, and a broken passage in which Hebat sees the king restored on Mount Hazzi; the end (whether Ullikummi is destroyed or transformed) is lost — the final scenes are a scholarly reconstruction from joins.

FUNCTIONS. The Song is the Hittite theology of succession and threat: Kumarbi's counter-creation (stone against storm) dramatizes the danger of sterility and inertia; Upelluri's aching shoulder aitiologizes the weight of the cosmos on its foundation; the reed-knife grounds the principle that the primal act of separation can be repeated to unmake threats; and the myth's Greek parallel (Ouranos-Kronos-Zeus; Atlas; the Typhon campaign) makes it the key comparandum in Near Eastern-Greek myth studies.
narrative.zh: 《烏利庫米之歌》：庫馬爾比被特舒卜廢黜，坐而謀亂；赴烏爾吉斯巨巖，右手左足按石而孕之；助產神女接生石嬰，庫馬爾比喜曰：『我為特舒卜造一對手……其名烏利庫米。』遂託聾盲石巨於沉睡巨人烏佩魯里肩上，暗中生長。日神巡天見海中異高，報特舒卜；特舒卜登哈齊山望之：石塔已高過山嶺。雷電不克，心如鉛熔；伊什塔爾歌之而石聾不聞。埃亞降至烏佩魯里問之，巨人呻曰：『昔天地築於我肩，我一無所知；今右肩微痛。』埃亞遂入上古神庫，得昔日分天地之銅刀，斷巨人足與肩之連結——巨人失其基而可戰。特舒卜驅車，風雷隨行，與聾石巨決戰，擲之於海——泥板至此而斷；勝負之末與結局由學界據殘片重構。功能：繼承與威脅之神學、宇宙重量之釋義（烏佩魯里肩痛）、原初分離之刃可再施之理、以及希臘神話比較之樞紐。

functions: Theology of succession: counter-creation (stone vs. storm) as deposition strategy
Cosmological aition: Upelluri's aching shoulder as the weight of heaven and earth
Principle of unmaking: the primal separation-knife can be reapplied
Greek comparandum: castration-succession, Atlas, and Typhon parallels with Hesiod

title.en: The Birth of Huitzilopochtli at Coatepec and the Defeat of Coyolxauhqui
title.zh: 威齊洛波奇特利於科阿特佩克山降生與科約爾沙赫基之敗

region.en: Coatepec ('Serpent Mountain'), symbolic pin at Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, Mexico City
region.zh: 科阿特佩克『蛇山』；象徵性定位於墨西哥城大神廟

texts.period: Recorded 16th c. CE: Florentine Codex (Sahagun, 1575-77, Book 3); Codex Chimalpopoca/Anales de Cuauhtitlan; principal MS: Florentine Codex, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Mediceo Palatino 218-220

source.archive: Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana (Florentine Codex) / scholarly translation (Dibble & Anderson)
source.work: Florentine Codex Book 3 (The Origin of the Gods), trans. A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble, Santa Fe 1957; Codex Chimalpopoca, trans. John Bierhorst, Tucson 1992

texts.license: 16th-c. sources public domain; modern translations quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Coatlicue, sweeping the serpent mountain, conceives from a ball of quetzal feathers; her daughter Coyolxauhqui and the four hundred southern stars plot her death; at the moment of birth the child Huitzilopochtli springs up fully armed, beheads Coyolxauhqui, and scatters the four hundred — the charter myth of war, sacrifice, and the Templo Mayor.
summary.zh: 科阿特利圭掃蛇山，得羽球而孕；女科約爾沙赫基與南方四百星神謀殺其母；臨產之際，威齊洛波奇特利全副武裝躍出，斬母姊之頭，驅散四百眾——此為戰爭、犧牲與大神廟之憲章神話。

sensitivity.note: Sources are colonial-era codices; living Nahua communities treat this heritage respectfully. Modern excavations at the Templo Mayor are Mexican national heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1: Coatlicue, our mother, was sweeping at Coatepec; a ball of feathers fell before her; she took it and placed it at her waist and was found with child; her sons said: 'Who has done this? She has dishonored us.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1 (ending): Just as Coyolxauhqui reached the summit, Huitzilopochtli was born, adorned with his shield, darts, and the blue serpent-sandal; he seized the turquoise serpent and struck his sister's head from her, and it fell below the mountain; he pursued and routed the four hundred, who became the stars. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1 (ending); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, Book 3, Santa Fe 1957 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE CONCEPTION. The goddess Coatlicue ('Serpent Skirt'), mother of the gods, sweeps the temple on Coatepec ('Serpent Mountain') near Tula; a ball of quetzal feathers (some versions: white feathers) descends before her; she tucks it into her waistband and is found pregnant. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui ('Painted with Bells'), mistress of the moon or of the dismembered, gathers the four hundred sons — the Centzon Huitznahua, the 'four hundred of the south' (stars of the southern sky) — and plots to kill their mother in shame: 'Who has done this? She has dishonored us!' Coatlicue hears them coming and trembles; the child in her womb speaks: 'Do not fear, mother; I know what I must do.'

MIDDLE: THE BIRTH IN ARMS. A messenger (Quauitlicac) runs ahead warning the besieged goddess; Coyolxauhqui leads the four hundred up the mountain, armed in ranks. At the moment of crisis, Huitzilopochtli ('Hummingbird of the South') is born — full-grown, armed with his shield (teueuelli), darts (tlacalhuaztli? tin? the atlatl darts), and the blue serpent-sandal (xiuhcoatl, the fire-serpent), painted with his war-paints (tlael? 'the refuse-smeared one' — tlaelquani, eater of filth, his ritual epithet). He seizes the xiuhcoatl and strikes Coyolxauhqui, cutting her head from her body; the head rolls down Coatepec and lands at their mother's feet. Huitzilopochtli chases the four hundred down the mountain slopes, routing them into the sky; those who die at his hand become the stars, and their scattered limbs were carved on the stone disk later found at the Templo Mayor.

END: THE TEMPLE AND THE RITUAL. The victory founds the sanctuary of Coatepec, and Huitzilopochtli takes the name Tetzahuitl Huitzilopochtli ('the terrifying one') — 'the people built the temple for him'; the goddesses who remained (Coyolxauhqui's sisters) mourn, and the ritual calendar builds on the battle: the festival of Panquetzaliztli raised banners to Huitzilopochtli; the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan reproduced Coatepec — Huitzilopochtli's temple on the south side, with the Coyolxauhqui disk at the stair's foot where sacrificed captives 'fell' like the moon-goddess; the serpent head at the temple's base marked the mountain. In 1978, excavations beneath Mexico City recovered the great Coyolxauhqui disk — the myth verified in stone.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter of Aztec warfare and sacrifice: the sun/star battle mapped the sky (southern stars routed daily by the rising sun — in some tellings Huitzilopochtli as solar god), the sacrificial victim's fall down the temple stair re-enacted Coyolxauhqui's fall, and the Templo Mayor's twin shrines (rain/Tlaloc and war/Huitzilopochtli) reproduced the mythic mountain in urban stone. The 'four hundred' became the classifier of military units (the Centzon), and the hummingbird-god the patron of migration — the god who led the Mexica from Aztlan to Tenochtitlan.
narrative.zh: 母神科阿特利圭於圖拉附近蛇山掃殿，羽球自天而降，納於腰間而孕。女科約爾沙赫基聚南方四百子（南天星神）謀弒母：『誰人所為？辱及吾族！』腹中子聞聲曰：『母勿懼，我知所為。』信使夸維特利卡克先行報信；科約爾沙赫基率四百眾執械上山。危急之際，威齊洛波奇特利（『南方之蜂鳥』）誕生——全身戰妝，持盾、飛鏢與藍蛇靴（修修科阿特爾火蛇）；執蛇擊其姊，斷其首，首滾落山下至母足之前；遂驅四百眾下坡，四散者化為群星。山頂遂立神殿，尊號『可畏者』。特諾奇蒂特蘭大神廟即蛇山之復刻：南殿奉戰神，階下置科約爾沙赫基石盤，犧牲者自階上滾落如月神之墜；1978 年墨西哥城地下發掘得此石盤。功能：戰爭與犧牲之憲章、日月星之天象釋義、大神廟雙殿（雨神與戰神）之山形復刻、以及四百之軍制分類。

functions: Charter of Aztec warfare and sacrifice: the victim's fall re-enacts Coyolxauhqui's
Solar theology: the rising sun routing the four hundred southern stars
Urban replication of myth: Templo Mayor as Coatepec, Coyolxauhqui disk at the stair
Migration cult: Huitzilopochtli as guide of the Mexica from Aztlan

title.en: Lac Long Quan and Au Co: The Dragon and the Fairy of a Hundred Eggs
title.zh: 貉龍君與嫗姬：龍父仙母百卵之裔

region.en: Phu Tho province (Hung Temple sanctuary; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 越南富壽省雄王廟（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Recorded in Linh Nam chich quai (14th c.); Dai Viet su ky toan thu (Ngo Si Lien, 1479); Hung Temple cycle living ritual

source.archive: Scholarly editions / Nghien cuu Viet Nam resources
source.work: Linh Nam chich quai (14th c.); Dai Viet su ky toan thu, Book 1 (Ngo Si Lien, 1479); scholarship: Keith W. Taylor, The Birth of Vietnam, Berkeley 1983

texts.license: Ancient texts public domain; modern translations quoted only as summary

summary.en: Lac Long Quan, the dragon lord of the waters, clears the land of monsters, marries the mountain fairy Au Co, who lays a sac of a hundred eggs; fifty children follow the father to the sea, fifty the mother to the mountains; the eldest becomes Hung Vuong, first of the Hồng Bàng kings — the charter of the Vietnamese people (children of dragon and fairy).
summary.zh: 水澤之龍君貉龍君掃除妖魔，娶山仙嫗姬；嫗姬產卵百枚；五十子隨父入海，五十子隨母上山；長子為雄王，開鴻龐氏——越南人『龍子仙孫』之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the Hung Kings' festival (national holiday) and the Hung Temple cult; nationalist ideology uses the narrative — handle critically.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Linh Nam chich quai narrative: Lac Long Quan, son of the dragon Kinh Duong Vuong, rid the land of the fish-monster Ngu Tinh, the nine-tailed fox Ho Tinh, and the tree demon Moc Tinh; he married the mountain fairy Au Co, who laid a sac of a hundred eggs, from which a hundred sons hatched. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Linh Nam chich quai narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the division (Toan thu 1479): The dragon lord said: 'I am of the dragon line, thou of the fairy line; water and mountain differ' — and they divided the hundred sons: fifty with the father to the deeps, fifty with the mother to the highlands; the eldest was crowned Hung Vuong at Phong Chau, and the country named Van Lang. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the division (Toan thu 1479); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Scholarly summaries via Taylor 1983 and Vietnamese editions (copyright); ancient texts public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE MONSTER-SLAYER. Lac Long Quan ('Dragon Lord of Lac'), son of Kinh Duong Vuong (the water-line of the South Sea dragon), roams the land and clears it of its monsters: the fish-monster Ngu Tinh of the sea (slain with? driven out with nets and rams? — the variants give his three monster-battles: Ngu Tinh the fish, Ho Tinh the nine-tailed fox of the mountains, Moc Tinh the tree demon of the forests), founding the order of the settled world.

MIDDLE: THE MARRIAGE AND THE HUNDRED EGGS. Lac Long Quan marries Au Co, the mountain fairy descended from the highlands; she lays a sac of a hundred eggs, from which hatch a hundred sons — the first Vietnamese. But the dragon of the waters and the fairy of the mountains cannot dwell together: 'I am of the dragon line, you are of the fairy; water and mountain differ; we cannot be forever joined.'

END: THE DIVISION AND THE HUNG KINGS. They divide the children: fifty follow the father into the sea-country (the coastal and riverine Lowlands — the Lac peoples), fifty follow the mother into the highlands (the mountain peoples); the eldest son is crowned Hung Vuong at Phong Chau (Phu Tho), founding the Hong Bang dynasty and the kingdom Van Lang — the first Vietnamese state. The narrative is the charter of Vietnamese identity: 'con Rong chau Tien' (children of Dragon, grandchildren of Fairy) — the unity of lowland and highland, water and mountain, in one descent; it is ritually grounded at the Hung Temple sanctuary (Phu Tho), where the Hung Kings' Festival (10th day of the 3rd lunar month, national holiday) renews the covenant; the national symbol (the dragon of Hanoi's? the descending-dragon Ha Long Bay aition is attached to the same dragon-line).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Vietnamese ethnic charter (dragon-fairy descent), the lowland-highland political synthesis (the fifty-fifty division), the Hung Temple cult (national pilgrimage), and the historiographic construction of antiquity (Toan thu 1479's editorial framing against Chinese 'Kija? ' claims — the Vietnamese response to Korea-style foundation legends). Scholarship (Taylor 1983) reads the cycle as 15th-century state ideology projected onto prehistoric materials — the record keeps both the mythic and the historiographic frames.

RITUAL AND RECEPTION. The Hung Temple sanctuary on Nghia Linh mountain (Phu Tho) holds the Hung Kings' Festival each year on the tenth day of the third lunar month — a national holiday since 2007 — when processions climb the 225 steps to the Upper Temple, offering chung and giay cakes (the square and round rice cakes of the Lang Lieu legend, the same dynasty's culinary charter). The Hung Kings' worship was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2012) as 'belief? a belief of the Vietnamese people'. In the modern state the narrative is taught as the first lesson of national history, and its fifty-fifty division is invoked in highland-lowland policy discourse; the dragon of the descent descends further in Hanoi's Thang Long ('ascending dragon') aition and Ha Long Bay's pearl-islands — one dragon-line, three geographies.
narrative.zh: 貉龍君為涇陽王（南海龍系）之子，遍行國土驅除三妖：海中魚精吳精、山中九尾狐狐精、林中樹妖木精，立定居之世。後娶山仙嫗姬；嫗姬產卵百枚，孵出百子——越南人之始祖。然龍屬水、仙屬山，二者難久居：『我為龍種，爾為仙種，水土不同，難合久居。』遂分百子：五十隨父入海居低地（貉人），五十隨母上山居高土；長子立於峰州為雄王，開鴻龐之世，國號文郎——越南第一國。此為越南民族認同之憲章：『龍子仙孫』——低地與高地、水與山之一系同源；富壽雄王廟為其聖地，雄王祭（三月初十，國定假日）年年更新盟約；下龍灣『龍降』之釋義亦屬同龍系。功能：民族族源憲章、低地高地政治綜合（五五之分）、雄王廟朝聖、以及1479年《大越史記全書》之國家意識形態建構（Taylor 1983 之批判讀法——十五世紀國家意識形態投射於史前素材）。

Lowland-highland synthesis: the fifty-fifty division as political geography
Hung Temple cult and the Hung Kings' Festival (national holiday, 3rd month 10th day)

title.en: Baal and the Sea-Dragon Yam
title.zh: 巴力與海龍雅姆

region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

texts.period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 2), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), summary of the Baal epics

summary.en: Yam, the tyrant Sea, commands the assembly of the gods to surrender Baal; crafty Kothar makes Baal two clubs that leap from his hand and split the tyrant — but the singers warn that the dragon Lotan, the wriggling seven-headed serpent, is not utterly slain, for Mot will one day swallow the storm-god in his turn.
summary.zh: 暴君海神雅姆迫眾神廷交出巴力；巧匠科塔爾為巴力鑄雙棍，躍出手而擊碎暴君——然歌者言：盤繞之七首巨龍羅坦未嘗盡誅，死神莫特他日必反噬風雨之神。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets excavated from 1929; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Yam the sea-tyrant sent to the divine assembly his demand that the gods deliver Baal to him, and the gods hid beneath their thrones; Astarte reproved them, and the craftsman Kothar wa-Khasis forged for Baal two Clubs which he named. The Club leapt from Baal's hand and smote Yam on the skull, and the tyrant Sea collapsed — and Baal reigned in his place.

[Condensed paraphrase] The singers warned: when you smite Lotan, the fleeing serpent, take his everlasting dominion from him — for Lotan the wriggling serpent, the seven-headed dragon, would rise again; and the day would come when Death himself, Mot, would swallow the storm-god who had conquered the Sea.

title.en: Baal Swallowed by Mot, and Restored
title.zh: 巴力入莫特之口而復生

region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

texts.period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 5-6), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), the first and second 'Alein Baal' epics

summary.en: Death, Mot, swallows Baal — the rains fail and the earth withers; his sister Anat finds the corpse, grinds Death in the sieve of her winnowing-fan, and the sun-goddess Shapash carries Baal back; seven years the devourer of the world lies crushed — and when Mot returns, the two are parted only by the terror of Shapash.
summary.zh: 死神莫特吞噬巴力——雨澤斷絕，大地枯槁；其妹阿娜特尋得其屍，以揚穀之篩碎磨死神，日神沙帕什負巴力而歸；滅世之口被碾凡七年——莫特復來時，唯畏日神之威而二神相分。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Mot the devourer invited Baal to come down into his house, the pit of the heart of the earth; Baal went, and Death swallowed him. With the storm-god in the grave, the rains ceased, the fields withered, and the earth lay dry; El grieved on his throne that Baal was perished like a dead man from the earth.

[Condensed paraphrase] Anat came down and found the body; she seized Death her brother, split him with the sword, winnowed him with the fan, burned him with fire, and ground him like grain for the birds. Then Shapash the sun-goddess lifted Baal from the pit and set him on his throne — and the rains returned; when Mot rose again seven years later, the terror of Shapash kept the two gods apart, and Baal's reign over the wet winds of the sky was secure.

title.en: Danel and the Murdered Hero Aqhat
title.zh: 但以理族長丹尼爾與被害英雄阿卡特

region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

texts.period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 17-19), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: James A. Montgomery, 'The Danel Text', Journal of the American Oriental Society, vol. 56 (1936), pp. 440-445

summary.en: The righteous king Danel, childless for seven years, prays and is granted a son, Aqhat — whom the craftsman Kothar equips with a wondrous bow; the goddess Anat covets the bow, and when the boy refuses to sell or give it, she slays him on the wings of the wind — and the birds of heaven bury the hero, while his sister Pughat takes up the avenger's place.
summary.zh: 義王丹尼爾無子七年，禱而得子阿卡特；巧匠科塔爾為其造神弓。女神阿娜特欲得此弓，少年拒售與贈，遂遭女神弒於風翼之上——天上群鳥葬英雄；其妹普珥特執報仇之職。
