passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Danel the righteous ruler of the assembly offered food to the gods and clothed the holy ones; seven years he had no son. On the seventh day Baal heard and moved El, and the god blessed the king: a son should be born to his house — and the child Aqhat was born to him, fed on the milk of the assemblies of the holy ones.

[Condensed paraphrase] Kothar the smith made the boy a bow of wonderful craft; Anat the huntress desired it, offering silver and gold, then the gift of immortality itself, but Aqhat refused her, saying the bow was for a warrior and not for a goddess to carry. In fury she cast him from the wings of the wind, and he became as a piece of the clouds; the eagle of the sky carried the tale to the grieving king, and his sister Pughat dressed as a man to take vengeance at the feasts of the murderer.

title.en: The Ramakien: Phra Ram and Thotsakan
title.zh: 拉瑪堅：帕拉姆與托薩根

region.zh: 泰國大城／曼谷

texts.period: Ramakien, Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; court recensions of the 18th-19th c. from older tradition

source.work: Ramakien (Thai: Ramakien), King Rama I's court recension, Thai original (e.g. Book 2, the war of Maiyarab)

summary.en: Thailand's Ramayana: Phra Ram, exiled with his bride Sida, loses her to Thotsakan the ten-faced giant-king of Longka; the monkey-general Hanuman builds the causeway of stones across the sea, Nonthok the demon's legend is fought, and the war of the city of fire ends with the trial of the faithful wife — the national myth told in murals, dance, and puppet theatre.
summary.zh: 泰國羅摩衍那：帕拉姆攜妻西達出亡，西達為龍卡國十面巨靈王托薩根所擄；神猴哈奴曼築石堤跨海，大戰焚城，終以貞后之火試為結——壁畫、舞劇與皮影相傳之國家神話。

sensitivity.note: Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; passages are condensed paraphrases of the court Ramakien recensions. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phra Ram, heir of Ayutthaya, went into the forest at his father's word with his brother Phra Lak and his bride Sida; the giant-king Thotsakan of Longka, ten faces and twenty arms, carried Sida across the sea, and the war of the Ramakien began.

[Condensed paraphrase] Hanuman the son of the wind, white monkey of a thousand wiles, gathered the armies of the monkeys, carried the mountain of healing herbs, and built the causeway of stones to the island of Longka; Phra Ram slew Thotsakan at last with the arrows of the gods — and the murals of Wat Phra Kaew and the khon dance tell the war still as the royal myth of Thailand.

title.en: Khun Borom and the Origin of the Tai Princes
title.zh: 坤博隆與泰人諸王之始

region.en: Muang Theng (Plain of Jars region), Laos/Thailand tradition
region.zh: 猛騰（川壙高原一帶，寮泰傳統）

texts.period: Tai/Lao origin myth; recorded in the 15th-19th c. chronicles (Urangadom, Nan chronicle)

source.work: G. E. Gerini, Researches on Ptolemy's Geography of Eastern Asia (Royal Asiatic Society/RGS, 1909), on Muang Then

summary.en: In the Tai origin cycle the sky-lord Khun Borom, seeing the earth waste and comfortless, sends down his seven sons from the heavenly city with buffalo, rice-seed, and teachers of the arts; the youngest, Khun Lo, takes the plain of the middle lands, and from the seven sons the princes of the Tai and Lao states trace their royal blood.
summary.zh: 泰人創世傳說：天君坤博隆見大地荒蕪，遣七子自天城而下，攜水牛、稻種與百工之師；幼子坤羅居中原之野——泰、寮諸國王族皆自七子溯其王統。

sensitivity.note: Tai/Lao foundational myth from the court chronicles; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Khun Borom the lord of the sky looked down on the world of men, which lay without order and without comfort; he sent down his seven sons, each with the gear of rule: buffaloes, seeds of rice, smiths and teachers, that the wild lands might be peopled and tilled.

[Condensed paraphrase] The sons built cities and ruled the countries of the Tai; Khun Lo the youngest took Muang Sua on the middle river, and his line the Lao kings traced. When the work was done the princes returned to the sky-city to report, and went down again with the mandate of Khun Borom to rule — the pattern of every Tai royal chronicle.

title.en: The Naga of the Mekong and the Fire-Balls of the River
title.zh: 湄公河龍王與河上火箭

region.zh: 湄公河（泰國廊開／永珍）

texts.period: Isan/Lao river legend of the Mekong naga

source.work: J. Ph. Vogel, Indian Serpent-Lore: The Nagas in Hindu Legend and Art (1926), on naga beliefs in the river-lands of Siam

summary.en: The great serpent Phaya Nak rules the deeps of the Mekong; in the river legend the naga's bride came from the water-country to the human world, and the serpent-king's tears and fire-balls rise from the river at the year's turning — the naga whose coils guard the Buddhist river-lands of the Lao and the Isan.
summary.zh: 巨蛇帕雅納克統湄公之深淵；河上傳說云蛇王之婦自水國適人間，歲末蛇王噴淚與火球自河面騰起——其身守護寮人與伊善地區之佛土江河。

sensitivity.note: Isan-Lao river legend; passages are condensed paraphrases. Living cultural heritage of the Mekong region. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phaya Nak, the great naga, ruled the deep channel of the Mekong from his city under the water; in the Isan legend his son loved a maiden of the human world and was given leave to serve the Buddha, guarding the river-lands with his coils.

[Condensed paraphrase] At the full moon of the eleventh month the naga is said to celebrate the end of the rains: columns of light and fire-balls rise from the river at Bang Fai, which the fishermen call the breath of the naga; the serpent-king remains the lord of the water-road of the Lao and Thai river country.

title.en: The Baal Cycle: Yam, the Palace, and the Defeat of Mot
title.zh: 巴力神話圈：雅姆、神殿與死亡之敗

region.zh: 敘利亞拉斯沙姆拉（烏加里特）

texts.period: Tablets excavated 1929-; composition c. 14th-13th c. BCE; principal tablets RS 2.014 etc. (Louvre AO 17.094 series; National Museum of Damascus)

source.work: Baal Cycle, KTU 1.1-1.6 (CTU 1.1-1.6); English: J. C. L. Gibson, Canaanite Myths and Legends, Edinburgh 1978; Dennis Pardee, Stories from Ancient Canaan, 2nd ed., Atlanta 2018

texts.license: Cuneiform text public domain; modern translations quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Baal, the storm-god, defeats the sea-king Yam with two magic clubs, wins a palace on Mount Saphon after the widow-goddess Asherah intervenes, and is swallowed by Mot, lord of death; Anat kills Mot — splitting, burning, grinding, and sowing him — and Baal returns; the two powers meet in seven-year combat until Shapash the sun separates them.
summary.zh: 風暴神巴力以雙魔杖誅海王雅姆，經寡婦女神阿瑟拉說情得蘇鳳山神殿；後為死神摩特所吞；阿娜特誅摩特——以刀分之、以火焚之、以磨研之、於田播之——巴力遂歸；二神七年之戰，以太陽神沙帕什居中調停。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; significant for biblical scholarship.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of KTU 1.2.iv: Kothar-wa-Hasis names the clubs — 'Yagrush (Chaser): chase Yam... Ayamur (Scatter): scatter Yam'; the clubs fly, and Yam falls; Baal proclaims: 'I have surely smitten Yam, the beloved of El... surely Baal reigns!' Not verbatim.

El dreams that Baal lives; Baal returns to his palace; Mot, restored, claims the fight again — and Shapash parts them. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Baal Cycle — six tablets found at Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria) in 1929-31 — is the fullest Canaanite narrative and the essential comparandum for biblical storm-theology.

TABLET 1-2: BAAL VERSUS YAM. The sea-king Yam (Sea, 'Prince Yam, the beloved of El') tyrannizes the divine assembly and demands Baal delivered as his slave. The gods cower; even El counsels compliance. Baal seizes weapons and would kill the messengers in the assembly; Asherah, the mother of the gods, intervenes — 'why do you kill the messengers?' — and pledges to secure Baal's freedom by persuading El to concede Yam's kingship in exchange for a palace? (In KTU 1.1, Asherah promises Yam gifts, including a palace, if he lets Baal live.) The craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Hasis forges two clubs and names them as spells: 'Yagrush (Chaser): chase Yam!' — the club flies and fails; 'Ayamur (Scatter): scatter Yam!' — Yam falls dead at Baal's feet. Baal proclaims his reign: 'surely Baal reigns over the gods'; Yam's scattered body is threshed (in some readings the sea's fishing aition: 'fish are his tribute').

TABLET 3: ANAT'S VENGEANCE. Anat, Baal's sister, the virgin warrior, slaughters the men of the towns who wronged her guests (the gruesome interlude), and exchanges messages with Baal about her powers ('I have a word of the tree, the whisper of the stone... which no man knows'); Baal promises to reveal the secret if she brings word of the? — Anat, pacified, proposes the palace project.

TABLET 4: THE PALACE ON SAPHON. Baal has no house like the other gods; Asherah goes to El, walks across his? and secures the grant: 'A house for Baal like his brothers' — Kothar builds on Mount Saphon with cedars from Lebanon and gold, silver, lapis. Kothar offers to install windows: Baal refuses — through a window Yam's agents (or demons) would come; he promises? finally concedes; windows are opened, and storm passes through them ('Baal opened windows in the house, a rift in the clouds') — the aition of the rain through the clouds. Baal celebrates, and the hymn of his triumph: 'Baal's word is secret? ' He copulates with a heifer (in some tellings his own? as bull), begets Magar ('the Victory') — and visits Mot.

TABLET 5: MOT SWALLOWS BAAL. Mot, lord of death ('Divine Mot'), sits in the pit, his throat from earth to heaven ('one lip to the earth, one lip to the heaven'); Baal comes at his summons and is swallowed whole: 'Baal is dead... what will the people do?' El, on his throne, dreams; the rains stop; the world dries (the death of the storm-god is the death of rain). Anat buries Baal on Saphon, slaughters Mot's son? (in KTU 1.5, she 'seizes the son of Asherah? ' — she cuts Mot's? the rite: she kills 'Divine Mot's heir'? — standard reading: she buries Baal, slays his killers?), and mourns with Shapash, the sun-goddess, who collects the pieces.

TABLET 6: THE DEATH OF MOT AND THE RETURN. Athtar, 'the Morning Star', takes Baal's empty throne — but he is too small for it ('his head did not reach its top'). Anat finds Mot, seizes him, and performs the ritual execution: 'with a blade she split him, with a winnowing-fork she burned him, with millstones she ground him, in the field she sowed him — the birds ate his remains' — the farmer-god's death sown like seed. Seven years pass (in some tellings seven years of famine? the text: after seven years, Mot returns alive, complaining that he was slain 'as if a kid? '); El dreams that Baal lives; Baal returns, defeats the restored Mot in seven-year combat ('as Baal seized Mot... the two? '), until Shapash, the sun, intervenes: 'how can you fight the Word of the Strongest? Mot, hear: Baal has thy word? — the sun parts them, and the cycle closes with Baal restored and El's blessing.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle is the theology of the year: rain (Baal) versus drought (Mot) versus chaos-sea (Yam); it grounds Ugaritic kingship ideology (the palace of Saphon mirrors the royal temple), the cult of the ancestors and of Baal-Hadad at Ugarit, and — through biblical polemic (Baal and Asherah in Hosea, Elijah on Carmel) — the very vocabulary in which Hebrew monotheism defined itself.
narrative.zh: 巴力神話圈六板：海王雅姆暴虐神會，索巴力為奴；諸神懾服，阿瑟拉說情；工匠神科塔爾鑄雙杖，念咒而投：『追趕者，追雅姆！』『驅散者，碎雅姆！』雅姆斃，巴力稱王。阿娜特屠城雪恥，與兄論神力之秘。寡婦阿瑟拉往說埃爾，巴力得蘇鳳山建殿：黎巴嫩雪松、金銀青金；科塔爾欲開窗，巴力初拒，終許之——雲隙降雨之緣起。巴力化牛與牝牛合，生『勝利』。後赴死亡之主摩特之召，被其吞噬：其喉自地至天；巴力既亡，雨絕地枯。阿娜特葬巴力於蘇鳳山，與日神沙帕什同哀。星辰阿塔爾攝位而身小不能登。阿娜特擒摩特，以刀分之、以簸箕焚之、以磨研之、於田播之、飛鳥食之——死神如種被播。七年後摩特復生索戰，埃爾夢巴力猶存；巴力歸，與摩特七年之鬥，日神沙帕什止之：『汝安能與至強者之言爭？』巴力復位，埃爾賜福而終。功能：雨旱海三力之年環神學、王權神學（蘇鳳山殿即王廟之影）、以及希伯來聖經巴力論戰之詞彙源。

title.en: The Ramakien: Phra Ram in the Bangkok Recension
title.zh: 《拉瑪堅》：曼谷本之帕拉瑪

region.en: Bangkok (Wat Phra Kaew murals; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 泰國曼谷玉佛寺壁畫（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rama I recension completed 1797 (Bangkok); Wat Phra Kaew mural program 1782-1809; khon masked dance-drama court tradition

source.work: Ramakien, Rama I recension (1797); mural program of Wat Phra Kaew; scholarship: Klaus Wenk, studies of the Ramakien murals; Frank E. Reynolds & Mani B. Reynolds, Three Worlds According to King Ruang (for the Thai Buddhist frame)

summary.en: The Thai Ramayana: Phra Ram, exiled with Nang Sida and Phra Lak, loses Sida to the ten-faced demon king Thotsakan of Longka; with the monkey armies and Hanuman's leaps, he builds the bridge, destroys Thotsakan, and returns to rule Ayodhya — the Thai royal recension that legitimates the Chakri dynasty.
summary.zh: 泰版羅摩衍那：帕拉瑪與娘子西達、帕拉剋流放；西達為十面魔王托沙坎擄至楞伽；得猴兵與哈努曼之助，跨海建橋、誅托沙坎，歸阿逾陀而王——此為確認卻克里王朝正統之王家抄本。

Mareet transforms into a golden deer; Thotsakan, the ten-faced king of Longka, seizes her; the dying bird? the vulture? Sida drops her ornaments to mark the trail. Not verbatim.

Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Ramakien is Thailand's national Ramayana, recast from the Sanskrit epic through Khmer and Mon intermediaries and finalized in the Bangkok recension completed by King Rama I in 1797 — the founding cultural act of the new Chakri dynasty, whose kings take the regnal name Rama.

THE THAI TELLING. Phra Ram (Rama) of Ayodhya (Thai: Ayutthaya), son of King Thotsarot (Dasharatha) by Nang Kaosuriya, is exiled fourteen years when Nang Kaiyakesi (Kaikeyi) claims her boons; he departs with his wife Nang Sida (Sita) and brother Phra Lak (Lakshmana). In the forest of? at Khao? the demon Mareet transforms into a golden deer; Sida's demand and Phra Lak's reluctant departure let Thotsakan (Ravana), the ten-faced, twenty-armed demon king of Longka (Lanka), abduct her — pulling up the whole hut with the earth; the vulture Satabut (Jatayu) fights him dying. Phra Ram allies with the monkey kings Sukhrip (Sugriva) and the white monkey Hanuman — son of the wind, son of? his jaw? his tail of fire burns Longka after his capture (the Thai scene of Hanuman's burning tail). The monkey army builds the stone causeway to Longka (the aition of the Adamman? of the string of islands — the 'bridge' still named in Thai geography); the war rages: Kumphakan (Kumbhakarna), roused from his six-month sleep, devours armies before falling to Phra Ram's arrows; the demon prince Intharachit (Indrajit) conjures illusory Sidas and nearly breaks the siege; Phra Lak and the? are healed by the? — the Thai version multiplies the magical battles. At the last, Phra Ram faces Thotsakan: the demon's ten heads regrow as they fall, until the great bow Brahmastra? the arrow of? Phra Ram's arrow — the bow given by Phra Isuan (Shiva) — severs the head that cannot regrow, and Thotsakan falls; his brother Wiroon? Vibhishan (Thai: Phra Wiroon? Piphek) is crowned. Sida's fidelity is proven by fire (the Thai fire ordeal — she survives, and the couple return in the flying chariot Pul? the Pali? the pushpaka); the Khmer? the Bangkok recension ends with the ideal kingship of Phra Ram at Ayutthaya.

FUNCTIONS. The Ramakien is the charter of Thai kingship: Rama I's recension legitimated the new dynasty (kings named Rama I-X); the Wat Phra Kaew mural program (1782-1809) walls the royal temple with 178 scenes of the story — the king walks the myth daily; the khon masked dance-drama enacts it at court festivals; and Hanuman is the comic sacred center of Thai popular culture (statues, amulets, kickboxing gyms). The Thai recension localizes: place-names, costume, the Buddhist karmic frame (Thotsakan's virtue acknowledged; his green? his color-coding), and the royal theology of the devaraja.
narrative.zh: 《拉瑪堅》為泰國之羅摩衍那，經高棉與孟人中介，於1797年由拉瑪一世定稿——新卻克里王朝立國之文化大典，歷代國王皆號『拉瑪』。帕拉瑪（羅摩）遭後母凱伊雅凱西索諾而流放十四年，攜娘子西達與弟帕拉剋入林；魔馬里特化金鹿誘之，十面二十臂之楞伽魔王托沙坎連屋帶地擄走西達；神鷹薩塔布特力戰而死。帕拉瑪結盟猴王蘇格里與白猴哈努曼（風神之子）；哈努曼被擒，火尾燒楞伽城；猴軍壘石跨海建橋（泰地群島之釋義）。戰爭層疊：睡六個月方醒之魔將坤帕坎吞食軍旅而亡；魔子因塔拉吉特幻化西達亂敵；最後帕拉瑪以濕婆所賜神弓之箭斬托沙坎不能復生之首；弟皮佩克受封。西達過火驗貞，夫婦乘飛車歸國，帕拉瑪行理想之治。功能：泰王權之憲章（拉瑪一世至十世之號）、玉佛寺178幅壁畫環繞王寺、孔劇於宮廷節慶演出、哈努曼為泰國大眾文化之聖喜中心。
